messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Apr 15, 2008 at 8:23 PM, John Watkinson <watk...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  I am also attempting to parallelize total copy number analysis of a
>  large number of GWS5 chips (~1400). However, a file-locking mechanism
>  sounds like a difficult and involved approach that could retain some
>  bottlenecks. A workaround in the interim would be to associate a
>  unique number with each segment (or "sub-job") of the larger job (most
>  cluster engines make such a number readily available) and then use
>  this number to ensure that all files written are unique. A "merging"
>  phase could follow at the end to combine the results in to a single
>  result. That may be too much to ask of the ChromosomeExplorer, but at
>  least the regions.xls file could be reconstituted. This cluster step
>  is probably only needed for the segmentation step, as this is easily
>  the most time-consuming.

I was think of the multi-chip probe summarization methods (PLMs) when
I talked about the file locking mechanism.  Those algorithms write to
multiple files multiple times.  For the segmentation methods this is
less necessary since they (typically) operate and store data sample by
sample and even chromosome by chromosome.  See more comment below.

>
>  Henrik, do you have any tips as how one could go about introducing
>  this extra "cluster node number" parameter and propogating it through
>  to all files written during the segmentation process? As an
>  experiment, I naively ran the segmentation on a cluster by breaking up
>  the chips to be processed over 200 nodes. The nodes all had network
>  file system access to the results of the previous processing steps.
>  The analysis was successfully completed, but the nodes overwrote each
>  other's output files.

It sounds to me that you are using process() of the ChromsomeExplorer
for executing the segmentation.  That is mostly done for your
convenience.  However, for distributed processing like what you want,
use fit() of the CopyNumberSegmentationModel, e.g. CbsModel.  It
operates on one sample and one chromosome at the time and stores data
by sample and chromosome (stored as binary R files [*.xls]). In that
sense there are no concurrency/dead lock/overwriting issues.

Then, use getRegions() of the same CopyNumberSegmentationModel and the
same sample and chromosome to extract the regions.  That call will
call fit() as well, but if/since it is already processed it will just
load the "fit" structure from file.   In other words, if all samples
and chromosomes have been processed your "merger" can call
getRegions(..., arrays, chromosomes) to retrieve all identified
regions.  You can then also call writeRegions() to write them to file.

To generate the image files in parallel, you can use writeGraphs(...,
arrays, chromosomes).

See process() of ChromosomeExplorer, which is basically a wrapper for
the above, for more details.

Hope this makes it easier for you to do segmentation in parallel.

/Henrik

>
>  Thanks in advance for any suggestions.
>
>   John Watkinson
>
>  On Apr 9, 2:23 pm, Nicolas Stransky <nicolas.stran...@gmail.com>
>  wrote:
>  > On 9 avr, 00:56, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>  >
>  > > Hi.
>  >
>  > Hi Henrik,
>  > Thank you for your answer.
>
> >
>  > > First, it is often much faster to work toward a local drive than over
>  > > a network file system.  I say this, because quite a few people are one
>  > > a shared file system.
>  >
>  > Thanks for the advice, I will experiment on this. I am indeed working
>  > on a network filesystem, but it had never been a bottleneck until
>  > now.
>
> >
>  > > Second, about Avg[Cn]Plm: Yes, the underlying model is a single-array
>  > > model.  However, due to lack of time, I actually let it inherit from
>  > > the ProbelLevelModel class (just like RmaPlm) so that I could reuse
>  > > the whole load-fit-save framework.  This means it indeed loads data in
>  > > chunks of units across all arrays and then fit the data array by
>  > > array.  It is on my lengthy todo list to make this a truly
>  > > array-by-array implementation (the estimates will be the same).
>  >
>  > Does this mean that for each array to be fitted, all data from all
>  > arrays has to be read? Indeed I observed that most time was spent
>  > reading and writing data, according to these time summaries:
>  >
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Total time for all units across all 96 arrays:
>  > 77602.51s == 1293.38min
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Total time per unit across all 96 arrays: 0.04s/
>  > unit
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Total time per unit and array: 0.43ms/unit & array
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Total time for one array (1881415 units): 13.47min
>  > = 0.22h
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Total time for complete data set: 1293.38min =
>  > 21.56h
>  > 20080409 09:54:24| Fraction of time spent on different tasks: Fitting:
>  > 1.0%, Reading: 29.3%, Writing: 68.1% (of which 84.98% is for encoding/
>  > writing chip-effects), Explicit garbage collection: 1.5%
>
> >
>  >
>  >
>  > > Third, before discussing parallelization, there is one obvious thing
>  > > one can do to speed up the processing of chip types with single-probe
>  > > probeset.  For instance, in GenomeWideSNP_{5|6} all CN units are
>  > > single-probe units, but they are still treated as units with unit
>  > > groups/probeset in all ways what that means, e.g. loading data in
>  > > across arrays wrapped up in a nested list, pass it to the internal fit
>  > > function, the unwrap the estimates and store them to file.  This is
>  > > done although the chip effect estimates for single-probe probesets are
>  > > all identical to probe signals (and there is no across-array
>  > > parameters/modelling).  In other words, one can update the
>  > > ProbelLevelModel class, and more specifically the fit() method, to
>  > > become aware of single-probe units and just "copy and paste" the probe
>  > > signals array by array first.  Doing that will probably speed up the
>  > > fit() call substantially - probably twice as fast for the GWS5/6
>  > > chips.  This is on my todo list as well, but since it is a
>  > > low-priority for me, it is unlikely that it will make it up to the top
>  > > anytime soon.  You are more than welcome to contribute to this work.
>  > > If you do, please let me know.
>  >
>  > I can try to have a look at this once I am more familiar with the
>  > whole implementation but since fitting seems to account for only 1% of
>  > the time I think the issue may not be there in my case :)
>
> >
>  > > Fourth, another thing way down on my todo list is to add a
>  > > *bullet-proof* and *cross-platform* file-locking mechanism for writing
>  > > to files such that "one" has to wait for the file to be release before
>  > > writing to it. Next, fit() of ProbeLevelModel need to be updated to
>  > > not process the units chunks in order, but in a random order.  With
>  > > these two features on can have multiple hosts process the same
>  > > PLM/data set at the same time.  Again, contributions are most welcome.
>  > >  The file-locking mechanism is something that should be developed and
>  > > tested independently of aroma.affymetrix.
>  >
>  > That would help a lot indeed, but I don't think I can do it myself
>  > unfortunately.
>  >
>  > Best regards,
>  > Nicolas

messages.subject: Chromosome Explorer: data overwrite
messages.body_plain:
Dear Henrik

I have just run GLAD for Sty arrays in one xterm and for Xba arrays in
another xterm using ChromosomeExplorer. Now I realized that the
computation finishing last does overwrite the data for
ChromosomExplorer.onLoad.js.

The problem is that the two files:
- ChromosomExplorer.html
- ChromosomExplorer.onLoad.js
are located in directory "reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY"

Could you change this and put the two files in the subdirectories for
the corresponding arrays:
"reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping250K_Sty"
"reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping50K_Xba240"

This would be great and would solve the problem, probably not only for
me, see the discussion about parallelization.
(However, it does not solve the problem of computing individual arrays
and/or chromosomes in parallel)

It should be possible since I have just manually placed the two files
for Xba in the corresponding Xba subfolder and rerun
ChromosomeExplorer for Sty and placed the results in the Sty
subfolder.

Best regards
Christian

On 29 mar, 18:07, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> However, if you want troubleshoot further, here is what goes on.  When
> you apply the allelic-crosstalk calibration you will introduce a
> fraction of non-positive probe signals (this is because some
> homozygote SNPs have true allele signal zero for one of the alleles,
> and then we add noise, but also because some signals are very close to
> the signal-to-noise levels).  Some of the non-positive signals will
> carry through to the summarized signals, the averaging over 3-4 SNP
> probes lower the fraction, but some still gets through.  For CN probes
> you will also get some non-positive signals.   The fragment-length
> normalization is modeling the data on the log2 scale, meaning
> non-positive signals will be NAs.  This is normally not a problem
> because there should be enough of finite log2 signals tofitthe

> effects.  However, for multi-enzymechip types such as GWS5 and GWS6,
> we stratify on loci exclusively on oneenzyme, and because a large

> fraction of loci are on both enzymes we have a smaller pool tofitthe
> model.  If you then have NAs in your data, the number of data points
> gets even smaller.   In your case the intersect of valid data points
> and loci exclusively onEnzyme#2 is zero.

>  (...)

> Moreover, there is an option to add a small offset to data before
> taking the log, e.g.
>
> fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(cs, shift=+200)
> fcns <- getTargetFunctions(fln, force=TRUE, verbose=-20)
>
> That might give you less NAs on the log2 scale.

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] RmaBackgroundCorrection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jay,

If you read that section of Ben's thesis carefully you will note that he refers to "the RMA convolution model background method".  In standard RMA, signal is modelled as normally distributed background convolved with exponentially distributed signal (see p 17-21 of the thesis).  The theta parameter referred to on page 24 is used in the "Low End Signal is Noise" (LESN) background correction method (see table 2.2) which is not part of standard RMA.  I never implemented this background method explicitly in aroma.affymetrix.  However, I believe there is a function in the affyPLM package (a package required by aroma.affymetrix) which implements it, and it should be fairly trivial to adapt RmaBackgroundCorrection() to take advantage of it.

Cheers,

Ken

>  Dear Henrik
>
>  I have just run GLAD for Sty arrays in one xterm and for Xba arrays in
>  another xterm using ChromosomeExplorer. Now I realized that the
>  computation finishing last does overwrite the data for
>  ChromosomExplorer.onLoad.js.
>
>  The problem is that the two files:
>  - ChromosomExplorer.html
>  - ChromosomExplorer.onLoad.js
>  are located in directory "reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY"
>
>  Could you change this and put the two files in the subdirectories for
>  the corresponding arrays:
>  "reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping250K_Sty"
>  "reports/Test/ACC,-XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping50K_Xba240"

Try to edit 'ChromosomExplorer.onLoad.js' so you get:

  this.setChipTypes(new Array('Mapping250K_Sty', 'Mapping50K_Xba240'));

because that is how it is designed to work.  However, for that to
work, your *.png files in the Mapping250K_Sty/glad/ and
Mapping50K_Xba240/glad/ must have the same format.

Of course, one could imaging that ChromosomeExplorer also generate
*.html, *.onLoad.js files in the chip type subdirectories, which could
then please both use cases.  I'll put it on the todo list, but I
cannot promise anything soon.

In order to avoid clashes, you can always add an extra tag, e.g.

ce <- ChromosomeExplorer(glad, tags="*,foo")
print(ce)

You must have done something else as well, because otherwise it won't
find the Javascript includes.

If you know the chromosome and the region you can query the
GenomeInformation file about the unit indices (as indexed by the CDF),
and then query the CDF for the SNP names of these units.  Example:

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("Mapping250K_Sty")
> gi <- getGenomeInformation(cdf)

# Units on Chr18 in 0-400kb
> units <- getUnitsOnChromosome(gi, chromosome=18, region=c(0,400e3))
> str(units)
 int [1:461] 1122 1692 1783 2593 3833 3864 5936 6065 6119 6374 ...

# Units on Chr18 in 0-200kb
> units <- getUnitsOnChromosome(gi, chromosome=18, region=c(0,200e3))
> str(units)
 int [1:165] 18620 21912 22288 24037 26680 30929 36893 40021 46805 51821 ...
> unitNames <- getUnitNames(cdf, units)
> str(unitNames)
 chr [1:165] "SNP_A-2174912" "SNP_A-1826004" "SNP_A-2079863" ...
> unitPos <- getPositions(gi, units)
> str(unitPos)
 int [1:165] 198147 121788 62481 165712 165407 165844 110632 190631 ...

You have to do the same for 'Mapping250K_Nsp' and then merge your data.

library(aroma.affymetrix);
